pack.name: Food Origins
pack.blurb: Ten true stories about where dinner came from.

puzzles.title: The Purple Carrot
puzzles.quote: Wild carrots were purple, not orange.
fact: Long before the carrot became the tidy orange stick in your fridge, it grew across Persia and Afghanistan as a thin, forked, strong smelling root. Wild carrots were purple, not orange. Farmers of the time valued the plant as much for its aromatic seeds and feathery leaves as for anything underground.

The orange carrot is a surprisingly modern invention. Dutch growers in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries kept selecting for a fatter, sweeter, less woody root, and the colour that came along for the ride was beta carotene. The vegetable we now treat as the definition of healthy eating is essentially a bred product of a few hundred years of patient gardening.

Purple carrots never actually vanished. They stayed in kitchens across Turkey, Iran and India, and they have quietly returned to European markets in the last twenty years, sold at a premium as something exotic and new.

puzzles.title: Chocolate Currency
puzzles.quote: Cacao beans were once used as actual money.
fact: Cacao beans were once used as actual money. Across the Maya and later the Aztec world, prices were quoted in beans the way we quote them in coins. A turkey might cost a hundred beans, a ripe avocado around three, and a day of a labourer's work perhaps the same again.

Anything valuable enough to spend is valuable enough to fake. Archaeologists have found hollow cacao husks carefully repacked with clay and mud, which is about the oldest counterfeiting scheme we have physical evidence for. Merchants learned to weigh and rattle their beans before agreeing to a deal.

The drink those beans became would be almost unrecognisable today. It was unsweetened, poured from height to raise a thick foam, and often spiked with chilli, vanilla or annatto. Sugar only entered the story much later, in Europe.

puzzles.title: The Jar That Never Spoiled
puzzles.quote: Honey sealed in ancient tombs is still edible.
fact: Honey sealed in ancient tombs is still edible. Excavators working in Egypt have opened pots left undisturbed for thousands of years and found the contents unspoiled, thick and golden, needing nothing more than a gentle warming to pour again.

The reason is chemistry rather than magic. Honey holds very little free water, which leaves nothing for bacteria to live on, and it is naturally acidic. Bees also add an enzyme that slowly releases tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Between them, those three defences make an environment almost nothing can grow in.
The one thing that will ruin a jar is moisture. Left open in a damp kitchen, honey absorbs water from the air and can finally ferment, which is exactly how mead was discovered.

puzzles.title: The Poison Apple
puzzles.quote: Europeans once feared the tomato as deadly poison.
fact: Europeans once feared the tomato as deadly poison. When Spanish ships carried it back from the Americas in the sixteenth century, botanists took one look at the plant and recognised the family. It was an obvious relative of deadly nightshade, so for well over a century the tomato was grown as an ornamental curiosity and kept firmly out of the kitchen.

There was also a genuine reason people fell ill. Wealthy households ate from pewter plates with a high lead content, and the acid in a tomato pulled that lead straight out into the food. The poor, eating from wood and clay, ate tomatoes happily and suffered nothing at all.

Naples eventually settled the argument. Poor southern Italian cooks put the fruit on flatbread because it was cheap and it kept well, and the dish they invented travelled the world under the name pizza.

puzzles.title: Two Years For One Fruit
puzzles.quote: One pineapple plant can take nearly two years to ripen.
fact: One pineapple plant can take nearly two years to ripen. It is a slow, spiky, unglamorous crop that produces a single fruit at the centre of a rosette of tough leaves, and once it has done so the parent plant is finished.

That slowness explains why the pineapple became a symbol of outrageous wealth in eighteenth century Europe. Growing one in a cold climate meant building a heated glasshouse and paying a gardener to nurse it for two years. A single fruit could cost the equivalent of a small house, so hosts displayed them rather than ate them, and there was a brisk trade in renting a pineapple for the evening.

There is a further oddity in the fruit itself. What looks like one pineapple is actually dozens of separate flowers that fused as they grew, which is why the skin is patterned in those tessellated hexagons.

puzzles.title: Berry Confusion
puzzles.quote: To a botanist the banana is a berry and the strawberry is not.
fact: To a botanist the banana is a berry and the strawberry is not. A berry has a strict definition: it grows from a single flower with one ovary, and it carries its seeds inside the flesh. Bananas, grapes, tomatoes and even cucumbers all pass that test comfortably.

A strawberry fails on every count. What you eat is a swollen flower base rather than an ovary, and the real fruits are the tiny specks on the outside, each one a separate seed carrier. The proper term is an aggregate accessory fruit, which is not something anyone wants printed on a jam label.

The banana plant is misfiled too. It is not a tree but the largest herb on earth, with a false trunk made of tightly wrapped leaf bases. Nearly every banana sold for export is a clone of a single variety, which is why one determined fungus can threaten the entire trade.

puzzles.title: Four Thousand Year Old Noodles
puzzles.quote: The oldest bowl of noodles ever unearthed was made from millet.
fact: In 2005 archaeologists digging at Lajia in north west China lifted an upturned earthenware bowl that had been buried by a flood roughly four thousand years ago. Underneath, protected by a pocket of air, sat a coil of thin yellow strands. The oldest bowl of noodles ever unearthed was made from millet.

That detail matters more than it sounds. Millet has almost no gluten, so those noodles could not have been rolled and cut in the familiar way. They were most likely pushed through a press or repeatedly stretched from a dough held together by sheer technique, which suggests a well developed cooking tradition rather than a first experiment.

The find did not settle the endless argument about who invented the noodle. Wheat noodles, Arab dried pasta and Italian pasta all have their own long histories and their own evidence, and the honest answer is that people in several places independently worked out that dough could be made into strings.

puzzles.title: Spuds In Space
puzzles.quote: A potato became the first food ever grown in orbit above our planet.
fact: A potato became the first food ever grown in orbit above our planet. In 1995 a joint experiment between NASA and the University of Wisconsin carried potato cuttings aboard the shuttle Columbia and produced tubers in weightlessness, proving that a crop could complete part of its life cycle away from the ground.

The potato was not a random choice. It yields more calories per square metre than almost anything else, it stores well, it grows from cuttings rather than seed, and nearly the whole plant is useful. Those are exactly the qualities you want when every gram of cargo is costed to the penny.

On earth the potato has done this before. Domesticated in the Andes thousands of years ago, where farmers still grow a startling range of shapes and colours, it later spread across Europe and quietly rewrote the population history of an entire continent.

puzzles.title: The Orchid In Your Ice Cream
puzzles.quote: Real vanilla comes from an orchid that must be pollinated by hand alone.
fact: Real vanilla comes from an orchid that must be pollinated by hand alone. The vine is native to Mexico, where a particular local bee had quietly done the job for centuries. Move the plant anywhere else in the world and the flowers open, wait a single morning, and close again having produced nothing.

The problem was solved in 1841 by Edmond Albius, an enslaved twelve year old boy on the island of Reunion, who worked out how to lift the flap separating the male and female parts of the flower and press them together with a sliver of bamboo. His method is still the method. Every vanilla pod in the world is the result of somebody performing that gesture, flower by flower, on the one morning it is possible.

Curing then takes months of blanching, sweating and slow drying before the pods develop any of the aroma we recognise. Between the hand work and the wait, vanilla remains the second most expensive spice on earth, which is why so much of what we taste is synthetic.

puzzles.title: Counted Grain By Grain
puzzles.quote: Black pepper was once so valuable that traders counted the grains one by one.
fact: Black pepper was once so valuable that traders counted the grains one by one. It arrived in Europe from the Malabar coast of India after a journey of thousands of miles, and it was weighed on delicate scales, written into wills, accepted for rent and used to settle debts between merchants.

When Alaric besieged Rome in 408, part of the ransom he demanded was three thousand pounds of pepper alongside the gold and silver. London dock workers handling pepper cargoes were later made to sew up their pockets, because a handful of what looks like dried seeds was worth stealing.

That single ingredient reshaped the map. The search for a sea route to the pepper ports pushed Portuguese ships around Africa and sent Columbus west by mistake, and the trading companies built on the spice run went on to govern territories larger than the countries that chartered them.

pack.name: Space and the Sky
pack.blurb: Ten true things about what is over your head.

puzzles.title: The Day That Outlasts The Year
puzzles.quote: A day on Venus is longer than its year.
fact: A day on Venus is longer than its year. The planet turns on its axis so slowly that one rotation takes about two hundred and forty three earth days, while a full lap around the sun takes only two hundred and twenty five.

It also turns the wrong way. Almost everything in the solar system spins in the same direction, a leftover of the disc it all condensed from, but Venus rotates backwards. Stand on the surface, if you somehow could, and you would watch the sun rise in the west.

Very little else about the place is welcoming either. The atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, the pressure at ground level is like being half a mile underwater, and a permanent haze of sulphuric acid cloud keeps the surface at around four hundred and sixty degrees.

puzzles.title: The Planet That Would Float
puzzles.quote: Saturn is light enough to float on water.
fact: Saturn is light enough to float on water. Averaged out across its enormous volume, the planet is less dense than water is, because it is essentially a very deep atmosphere of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface to stand on.

The picture of it bobbing in a giant bath is a useful lie rather than a real possibility. There is no bath large enough, the planet would tear itself apart under its own gravity long before it settled, and the dense core at the centre is anything but light.

The rings are stranger than the planet. They stretch across a span wider than the distance from here to the moon, yet in most places they are only about ten metres thick, and they are made almost entirely of ordinary water ice.

puzzles.title: The Moon Is Leaving
puzzles.quote: The moon drifts further from earth every year.
fact: The moon drifts further from earth every year. Mirrors left on the surface by the Apollo crews let us bounce a laser off it and measure the gap to within a few centimetres, and the answer keeps growing by about three and a half centimetres every year.

Tides are the reason. The moon raises a bulge of water on the earth, our spin drags that bulge slightly ahead, and the bulge tugs the moon forward into a wider orbit. The energy has to come from somewhere, so our own day gets a fraction of a second longer every century.

Run the film backwards and it gets dramatic. When the moon formed it may have been ten times closer, filling the sky, hauling tides hundreds of metres high across an earth that spun through a day in five or six hours.

puzzles.title: Almost Everything Is The Sun
puzzles.quote: The sun holds almost all the mass in the solar system.
fact: The sun holds almost all the mass in the solar system. Add up everything else, every planet and moon and asteroid and comet, and the total comes to about one seventh of one percent. Jupiter alone accounts for most of that remainder.

It is worth sitting with the scale for a moment. You could pour a million earths into the sun and still have room to spare, and the fusion running in its core turns roughly four million tonnes of matter into energy every second.
That imbalance is why the solar system works at all. Everything else is essentially debris orbiting one very large object, and the sun's gravity sets the timetable for all of it.

puzzles.title: Footprints With No Weather
puzzles.quote: Footprints left on the moon will last millions of years.
fact: Footprints left on the moon will last millions of years. There is no wind to blow the dust about and no rain to wash it away, so the marks pressed into the surface in 1969 are still sitting there in exactly the shape they were made.

They are not quite permanent. A steady drizzle of micrometeorites slowly churns the top layer of soil, and the sun's radiation gradually reworks the grains, so the prints will soften and vanish eventually. It simply takes a very long time.

The dust itself surprised the crews. Moon soil is sharp and glassy, produced by impacts rather than weather, and it clung to everything. It wore through the outer layer of their boots, smelled of spent gunpowder when it was brought inside, and got into every seal on the spacecraft.

puzzles.title: The Silence Out There
puzzles.quote: Space is completely silent because sound needs air to travel.
fact: Space is completely silent because sound needs air to travel. A sound is a pressure wave passing through a material, so with almost no material between the stars there is nothing to carry it. An explosion the size of a planet would reach you as light, never as noise.

Which makes every space film you have ever seen a polite fiction. Real footage from outside a spacecraft has no soundtrack at all, and astronauts on a spacewalk hear only their own suit: the fans, the radio, their own breathing.

There is a loophole. Thin gas between galaxies can still carry very low pressure waves, and astronomers have found the ringing of one in the Perseus cluster. Converted into something a human ear could use, the note sits about fifty seven octaves below middle C.

puzzles.title: A Spoonful Of A Dead Star
puzzles.quote: One teaspoon of neutron star matter would weigh a billion tonnes.
fact: One teaspoon of neutron star matter would weigh a billion tonnes. When a massive star runs out of fuel its core collapses so hard that electrons and protons are crushed together into neutrons, packing the mass of a sun into a ball the size of a city.

Everything about the result is extreme. The surface gravity is billions of times ours, the crust may be the strongest material in the universe, and some of these objects spin hundreds of times a second, sweeping a beam of radio waves past us like a lighthouse.
We owe them a debt. When two neutron stars collide they scatter freshly made heavy elements across space, and a good share of the gold and platinum on earth was probably minted in a crash like that.

puzzles.title: What Space Smells Like
puzzles.quote: The likely cause is chemistry clinging to the fabric.
fact: Astronauts describe the smell of space as faintly like seared steak. Nobody can smell the vacuum itself, but after a spacewalk the airlock repressurises and the suits come off, and crew after crew has reported the same odd mix of burnt meat, hot metal and welding fumes.

The likely cause is chemistry clinging to the fabric. Atomic oxygen, single atoms rather than the paired kind we breathe, sticks to everything outside and recombines once it is back in a warm cabin. Anything that has been sitting in raw sunlight is also very slightly scorched.

Different corners of space would smell different anyway. Clouds of gas where stars form are full of carbon compounds, and one near the centre of our galaxy contains ethyl formate, the ester that gives raspberries part of their flavour.

puzzles.title: Old Light Through The Window
puzzles.quote: Sunlight reaching your window began its journey thousands of years ago.
fact: Sunlight reaching your window began its journey thousands of years ago. The last eight minutes of the trip, from the sun's surface to here, is the easy part. Before that the energy spent an enormous stretch of time fighting its way out of the sun's interior.

The core is so dense that a packet of light cannot travel in a straight line. It is absorbed and thrown out again in a random direction over and over, drifting outward by accident rather than intent, and estimates for that stumble range from ten thousand to a hundred thousand years.
So a sunbeam on your desk is genuinely ancient. It was made while people were painting cave walls, and the energy in it has been trying to leave home ever since.

puzzles.title: You Are Made Of Old Stars
puzzles.quote: The heaviest atoms inside your body were forged long ago inside exploding stars.
fact: The heaviest atoms inside your body were forged long ago inside exploding stars. The early universe made almost nothing but hydrogen and helium. Every carbon atom in your cells and every iron atom in your blood was assembled later, in the crushing heat at the heart of a star.

Getting it out again takes a catastrophe. A big star spends millions of years building heavier elements in shells around its core, then collapses and detonates, flinging the whole inventory into space. That debris seeds the next generation of stars and planets.

Our own solar system condensed out of exactly such wreckage. The calcium in your bones, the oxygen in your lungs and the gold in a wedding ring are all second hand material, and every one of those atoms is older than the sun.

pack.name: The Human Body
pack.blurb: Ten true things about the machine you live in.

puzzles.title: Two Billion Beats
puzzles.quote: Your heart will beat two billion times.
fact: Your heart will beat two billion times. At a resting rate of about seventy beats a minute that works out at a hundred thousand a day, thirty seven million a year, and comfortably past two billion over an ordinary lifetime, without a single break for maintenance.

It is not a large organ. A fist of muscle, weighing about three hundred grams, moving roughly five litres of blood every minute and pushing it through a network of vessels that reaches every cell you own.

The tissue also has its own private plumbing. Blood inside the chambers is no use to the muscle wall, so a separate set of arteries wraps around the outside to feed the pump itself, which is why a blockage in one of them is such bad news.

puzzles.title: The Hardest Thing You Own
puzzles.quote: Tooth enamel is the hardest thing you own.
fact: Tooth enamel is the hardest thing you own. It is about ninety six percent mineral, harder than steel by some measures, and it has to be, because it spends decades grinding against itself under enormous force.

It has one serious design flaw. Unlike bone and skin, enamel contains no living cells at all, so once a piece is gone the body cannot make more. Every other tissue you have repairs itself. This one is a single lifetime allowance.

The damage is rarely mechanical. Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid, and acid dissolves the mineral. That is the whole story of tooth decay, and it is why the fluoride in toothpaste matters: it helps the surface put lost mineral back.

puzzles.title: A Brand New Cover
puzzles.quote: Your body makes new skin about every month.
fact: Your body makes new skin about every month. Cells are born at the base of the outer layer, are pushed slowly upwards as the ones above them die, flatten into a tough waterproof shield, and are then rubbed off entirely.

The scale of the shedding is unpleasant to think about. You lose somewhere around thirty thousand dead skin cells a minute, and a good share of household dust is exactly that. Over a year it adds up to several kilograms of you, quietly redistributed around the house.
Skin is also the largest organ you have, about two square metres of it. It keeps water in, keeps most microbes out, makes vitamin D out of sunlight and reports back on everything you touch.

puzzles.title: Fewer Bones Than A Baby
puzzles.quote: A human adult has fewer bones than a newborn baby.
fact: A human adult has fewer bones than a newborn baby. A baby starts with around three hundred separate pieces, many of them still soft cartilage, and an adult skeleton has two hundred and six. Nothing is lost along the way: they fuse.

The skull shows the trick most clearly. It arrives as several plates with gaps between them, which is what lets a head squeeze through birth and then keep growing, and the seams only knit together over the first couple of years.

Bone is also nothing like the dry object in a museum case. It is living tissue with a blood supply, it remodels itself constantly in response to the loads you put on it, and weight for weight it handles compression better than concrete.

puzzles.title: Half Of You Is Not You
puzzles.quote: Roughly half the cells in your body are not human at all.
fact: Roughly half the cells in your body are not human at all. Careful counts put the number of bacterial cells you carry at about thirty nine trillion against thirty billion human ones, which makes the split close to even.

They are not passengers. Gut bacteria finish digesting food your own enzymes cannot touch, make vitamins you need, train your immune system while it is still learning, and crowd out species that would do you harm.

Most of them live in the large intestine, and the whole community weighs about as much as your brain. Two people can carry wildly different mixtures, which is one reason the same meal can suit one person and defeat another.

puzzles.title: A Very Long Circuit
puzzles.quote: The blood vessels in one body would circle the earth twice.
fact: The blood vessels in one body would circle the earth twice. Laid end to end, the arteries, veins and capillaries of an adult run to something like a hundred thousand kilometres, and the planet is forty thousand around.

Almost all of that length is invisible. The famous vessels are the big ones, but the vast majority are capillaries thinner than a hair, and no cell in you sits more than a fraction of a millimetre from one.

The heart pushes blood around that circuit in under a minute. Pressure falls away as the pipes divide, which is the point: blood has to crawl through a capillary slowly enough to unload its oxygen and pick up the waste.

puzzles.title: The Brain On A Light Bulb
puzzles.quote: Your brain runs on about the same power as a household light bulb.
fact: Your brain runs on about the same power as a household light bulb. Roughly twenty watts keeps eighty six billion neurons talking to each other, which is a fifth of everything you burn in a day for something that weighs under one and a half kilograms.

No machine comes close on those terms. A computer asked to do a fraction of what you manage while walking down a street and recognising a friend would need a great deal more electricity and a serious cooling system.
The bill never stops either. Even in deep sleep the brain keeps spending, tidying, replaying and consolidating the day, which is part of why a night without it leaves you so useless.

puzzles.title: Lungs Laid Out Flat
puzzles.quote: Stretched flat your lungs would cover half of a tennis court.
fact: Stretched flat your lungs would cover half of a tennis court. The trick is not size but folding: each lung divides into ever smaller tubes ending in hundreds of millions of tiny sacs, and it is the total surface of those sacs that does the work.

Every one of them is wrapped in blood vessels so fine that red cells pass through in single file, and the wall between air and blood is a fraction of the width of a hair. Oxygen crosses it by simply drifting from where there is more to where there is less.
You move about ten thousand litres of air through that surface every day, in roughly twenty thousand breaths, and almost none of it takes any conscious thought at all.

puzzles.title: Nobody Else Has Your Print
puzzles.quote: Every person alive has a pattern of tongue prints as unique as fingerprints.
fact: Every person alive has a pattern of tongue prints as unique as fingerprints. The shape, the grooves and the arrangement of the surface differ from one mouth to the next, and researchers have built working identification systems around it.

Fingerprints are only the best known member of a large family. Irises, the veins in a palm, the pattern of a retina, the ridges of an ear and even the rhythm of a walk are all individual enough to tell people apart.

Identical twins make the point neatly. They share their entire genome, yet their fingerprints differ, because the ridges are shaped by the small physical accidents of growth in the womb rather than by the code alone.

puzzles.title: Signals At Traffic Speed
puzzles.quote: Nerve signals race along your body at more than a hundred metres every second.
fact: Nerve signals race along your body at more than a hundred metres every second. The fastest fibres, the thick ones wrapped in a fatty sheath, carry a message from your toe to your spine in a few hundredths of a second.

The sheath is what makes the speed possible. It insulates the fibre except at regular gaps, so the signal jumps from gap to gap instead of crawling along the whole length, which is both quicker and far cheaper in energy.

Not everything travels first class. Dull aching pain uses thin unwrapped fibres that plod along at a metre or two a second, which is exactly why you feel the sharp stab of an injury well before the deep ache arrives.

pack.name: The Ancient World
pack.blurb: Ten true things people did a very long time ago.

puzzles.title: The Cat Went First
puzzles.quote: Cats chose to live with farmers.
fact: Cats chose to live with farmers. Nobody domesticated them. Once people began storing grain, the stores drew mice, and the mice drew wildcats, and the deal was simply that the hunting was better near a village.

The oldest evidence of the arrangement is a grave in Cyprus, where a person and a cat were buried together nine and a half thousand years ago. Cyprus had no native wildcats, so somebody had carried that animal across the sea by boat.

The genetics show how little we changed them. Compared with dogs, cattle or wheat, the domestic cat is barely altered from its wild ancestor, which fits an animal that domesticated itself and never fully agreed to the terms.

puzzles.title: Rome Had Fast Food
puzzles.quote: Most people in Rome ate out every day.
fact: Most people in Rome ate out every day. Ordinary flats in the city had no hearth, because an open fire in a crowded timber and brick block was a good way to burn down the neighbourhood, so cooking happened elsewhere.

Elsewhere meant the counter on the corner. Excavations at Pompeii and Ostia turn up hundreds of little shops with masonry counters and sunken jars for hot food, selling stew, bread, cheese, olives and heavily watered wine to anyone passing.

The scale of the habit surprised the archaeologists who counted them. One street in Pompeii has a food counter every few doors, which puts ancient dining somewhere between a modern food court and a very busy pub.

puzzles.title: Steel Before Its Time
puzzles.quote: The chemistry only arrived much later.
fact: Craftsmen were forging fine steel long before anyone understood the recipe. Smiths in southern India were making crucible steel by the early centuries of the common era, sealing iron and carbon rich material in a clay pot and heating it for hours.

The bars travelled enormous distances. Traded west through Persia and the Arab world, they became the blades that Europe knew as Damascus steel, admired for holding an edge and for the watery pattern in the surface.

The chemistry only arrived much later. Nobody involved could have described carbon content or crystal structure, and the method was carried instead as a craft: exact clay, exact charge, exact number of hours, passed on by being shown.

puzzles.title: Older Than The Mammoth
puzzles.quote: Mammoths were alive when the pyramids were built.
fact: Mammoths were alive when the pyramids were built. The mainland herds had gone, but a stranded population survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean until about four thousand years ago, several centuries after the great pyramid at Giza was finished.

Isolation made them smaller and steadily less healthy. Cut off by rising seas at the end of the last ice age, the island group bred among itself for thousands of years and slowly accumulated the genetic faults that come with a tiny population.

The overlap is a useful reminder of how recent ancient history is. Written records, cities, taxes and monumental architecture all existed while a herd of mammoths was still walking around on the other side of the world.

puzzles.title: Paid In Bread And Beer
puzzles.quote: The workers who built the pyramids were paid in bread and beer.
fact: The workers who built the pyramids were paid in bread and beer. Records from the workers' villages list rations by the loaf and the jug, and the beer was thick, mildly alcoholic and nourishing enough to count as food rather than a treat.

They were not slaves. The camps beside the pyramids have bakeries, breweries, hospitals with mended bones and a cemetery of ordinary graves, all of which describe a large paid workforce rotating through in organised gangs.
The gangs even had names. Graffiti left inside the monuments records teams calling themselves things like the friends of Khufu, scrawled where nobody was ever supposed to look again.

puzzles.title: Painted, Not Pale
puzzles.quote: Greek statues were once painted in loud colours from head to toe.
fact: Greek statues were once painted in loud colours from head to toe. The white marble we admire in museums is simply stone that lost its paint, and traces of red, blue, yellow and gold survive in the grooves and folds where weather could not reach.

Modern light picks up what the eye cannot. Ultraviolet photography and raking light reveal patterns of decoration across statues that look bare, and reconstructions in full colour tend to shock people who grew up with the pale version.

That pale version shaped centuries of taste. Renaissance artists studied weathered marbles, concluded that restraint was the classical ideal, and built a whole aesthetic on what was really just a very slow loss of pigment.

puzzles.title: Complaints In Clay
puzzles.quote: The oldest written complaint is about a bad delivery of copper.
fact: The oldest written complaint is about a bad delivery of copper. A clay tablet from Ur, written around three and a half thousand years ago, carries a furious letter from a merchant called Nanni to a trader named Ea-nasir about ingots of the wrong quality and a messenger sent away empty handed.

It survives because of what it is made of. Fired or simply baked hard by time, a clay tablet outlasts paper, parchment and hard drives without any effort at all, which is why so much of the earliest writing we have is receipts, contracts and grumbling.
Archaeologists digging Ea-nasir's house found several other complaints stored in the same room. Nobody knows why he kept them.

puzzles.title: The Machine In The Wreck
puzzles.quote: A shipwreck gave up a bronze machine that predicted eclipses.
fact: A shipwreck gave up a bronze machine that predicted eclipses. Sponge divers working off the island of Antikythera in 1901 brought up a corroded lump that turned out to hold at least thirty interlocking gears cut by hand.

It is a model of the sky. Turn the handle and pointers show the sun and moon moving through the zodiac, the phase of the moon, the dates of eclipses and the cycle of the games, all driven by gear ratios chosen to match real astronomy.

Nothing of comparable complexity survives for more than a thousand years afterwards. Whatever workshop tradition produced it left no other trace, which is why a single corroded lump rewrote what we thought ancient engineers could do.

puzzles.title: Concrete That Heals
puzzles.quote: Roman concrete grows stronger in seawater instead of crumbling.
fact: Roman concrete grows stronger in seawater instead of crumbling. Harbour walls poured two thousand years ago are still standing, while modern reinforced concrete in the same conditions begins to fail within decades.

The recipe is the reason. Roman builders mixed volcanic ash with lime and seawater, and the reaction produced rare minerals that keep growing inside the cracks. Salt water that would destroy an ordinary wall feeds this one.

Recent work suggests the mixing was deliberately rough. Lumps of unslaked lime left in the mix act as a repair kit: when a crack lets water in, the lumps dissolve, and the gap fills itself with fresh mineral.

puzzles.title: The Library In The Ashes
puzzles.quote: A whole library of scrolls survived the eruption as blocks of charcoal.
fact: A whole library of scrolls survived the eruption as blocks of charcoal. When Vesuvius buried Herculaneum, a villa full of papyrus rolls was cooked rather than burnt, leaving hundreds of carbonised lumps too fragile to unroll.
Early attempts to open them destroyed dozens. The rolls crack into flakes at a touch, and for two centuries the collection sat in storage as the most tantalising unreadable text in the world.

It is being read now without being opened. High energy scans map the layers inside a lump, machine learning picks out the faint traces of ink, and the words are recovered line by line from a scroll that stays shut.

pack.name: The Animal Kingdom
pack.blurb: Ten true things about the neighbours.

puzzles.title: Holding Hands At Sea
puzzles.quote: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep.
fact: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep. Resting groups link paws into floating rafts, sometimes dozens of animals wide, which keeps families together and stops the tide carrying a sleeping otter out of the kelp bed.
They also anchor themselves. An otter will wrap a strand of kelp around its body before dozing, using the seaweed as a mooring line, and mothers park a pup in the kelp while they dive for food.

Almost everything about them is about warmth. Sea otters have no blubber, so they rely on the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs in a patch the size of a postage stamp, and they eat a quarter of their body weight a day to keep the furnace going.

puzzles.title: Three Hearts, Blue Blood
puzzles.quote: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. Two hearts push blood through the gills and the third sends it round the body, and the whole system runs on a copper based pigment rather than the iron based one we use, which is why the blood is blue.

That arrangement has a cost. The body heart stops beating while the animal swims, so swimming is exhausting and an octopus would rather crawl, which is exactly what it does whenever it has the option.

The nervous system is stranger still. Around two thirds of its neurons sit in the arms rather than the head, so each arm solves a good deal of the problem of where to go and what to grab largely on its own.

puzzles.title: Half A Brain Asleep
puzzles.quote: A dolphin sleeps with one half of its brain awake.
fact: A dolphin sleeps with one half of its brain awake. Breathing is a conscious act for a dolphin, so falling fully asleep would mean drowning. Instead one hemisphere rests while the other keeps watch, and a few hours later they swap.
You can see it from the outside. A resting dolphin often keeps one eye open, and the open eye belongs to the half that is currently on duty, scanning for company and for anything with teeth.

Newborns take the idea further. Calves and their mothers go almost without sleep for the first weeks of life, swimming constantly, and gradually settle into the half and half pattern as the calf grows.

puzzles.title: The Bird That Remembers You
puzzles.quote: A crow can remember a human face for years afterwards.
fact: A crow can remember a human face for years afterwards. Researchers who trapped and released crows while wearing a particular mask were scolded by the local birds for years, and by birds that had never been caught themselves.
That last part is the interesting bit. The grudge spreads socially: young crows learn which face is dangerous by watching adults mob it, so a reputation outlives the encounter that created it.

The rest of the toolkit is just as good. Crows make hooks from twigs, drop nuts on roads for cars to crack, plan a couple of steps ahead in laboratory puzzles, and appear to hold something close to a grudge in the ordinary sense of the word.

puzzles.title: Ants Beyond Counting
puzzles.quote: Every human on earth shares the planet with millions of ants.
fact: Every human on earth shares the planet with millions of ants. A careful global estimate puts the total at about twenty thousand trillion, which works out at somewhere over two million ants per person, and the combined weight of them exceeds that of all wild birds and mammals together.
They earn their keep. Ants turn over soil on a scale that rivals earthworms, carry seeds around, clear away dead insects and prune the plant world in ways that quietly shape entire habitats.

A colony behaves like one animal rather than a crowd. No ant is in charge and none has a plan, yet simple rules and chemical trails produce farming, herding, road building, warfare and organised rubbish disposal.

puzzles.title: Stripes Nobody Repeats
puzzles.quote: No two tigers anywhere wear quite the same pattern of stripes.
fact: No two tigers anywhere wear quite the same pattern of stripes. The markings work like a fingerprint, and researchers identify individuals from camera trap photographs by comparing the flank pattern rather than by tagging the animal.
The stripes are in the skin as well as the fur. Shave a tiger and the pattern is still there, because the pigment is laid down in the skin itself and the hairs simply follow the plan underneath.

As camouflage it is better than it looks. Vertical bars break up an outline in tall grass, and the animals a tiger hunts are mostly dichromatic, so to a deer that bright orange coat reads as a dull green.

puzzles.title: Cube Shaped Evidence
puzzles.quote: A wombat produces droppings shaped like little cubes.
fact: A wombat produces droppings shaped like little cubes. It makes around a hundred of them a night and stacks them on rocks and logs, where a flat sided pellet is far less likely to roll away than a round one.

The shape is made in the gut. The last stretch of intestine has stiff and stretchy sections in an uneven pattern, and as the very dry contents are squeezed along they are moulded into corners and flat faces.
The stacking is the point of the exercise. Wombats have poor eyesight and rely on smell to mark territory, so a cube parked on top of a rock at nose height is a message that stays where it was left.

puzzles.title: Older Than The Oldest Tree
puzzles.quote: A Greenland shark can live for hundreds of years in cold water.
fact: A Greenland shark can live for hundreds of years in cold water. Dating the lens of the eye gives ages of around four hundred, which makes it the longest lived animal with a backbone that we know of.

Everything about it is slow. The shark grows about a centimetre a year, cruises at less than one kilometre an hour, and is not thought to breed until somewhere around its one hundred and fiftieth birthday.
The cold explains a good deal of it. Life in near freezing Arctic water runs at a crawl, and a body that ages that gently has time to accumulate an extraordinary amount of history.

puzzles.title: A Tongue Heavier Than You
puzzles.quote: The tongue of a blue whale weighs about as much as a full grown elephant.
fact: The tongue of a blue whale weighs about as much as a full grown elephant. The animal itself reaches thirty metres and two hundred tonnes, which makes it the largest creature that has ever lived, larger than any dinosaur we have found.
The heart matches the scale. It is roughly the size of a small car, beats as slowly as twice a minute during a deep dive, and pushes blood through vessels wide enough for a child to crawl along.

All of it is built on some of the smallest food in the ocean. A feeding whale lunges through a swarm of krill, takes in a volume of water larger than its own body, and strains out several tonnes of shrimp the size of a fingernail every day.

puzzles.title: The Immortal Jellyfish
puzzles.quote: One jellyfish can reverse its own life cycle and begin again as a polyp.
fact: One jellyfish can reverse its own life cycle and begin again as a polyp. Under stress, injury or starvation, the adult of a small species called Turritopsis settles onto a surface and rebuilds itself back into the juvenile stage it grew out of.

Its cells simply change job. Muscle can become nerve, nerve can become something else, and the animal reassembles a younger version of itself out of the parts it already has, then grows up all over again.

It is not truly immortal. Predators, disease and a hungry fish end most of these lives well before the trick is needed, but in a tank with nothing to eat it a single animal has been sent round the loop repeatedly.
